subject: maths
title: Numbers to 20 - Odd, Even, Order and Money
introductionText:
Term 3 · Number
Numbers to 20 — Odd, Even, Order and
Money
The Big Idea: Even numbers can be shared into pairs with nothing left over; odd numbers
always have one left over. 1st, 2nd, 3rd tell us a position. Coins and notes are how we
count money.
Say It Like This
Read aloud
"Let's pair up the socks. Every sock has a partner — 6 socks make 3 pairs. 6 is an even
number. Now 7 socks: three pairs and one lonely sock. 7 is an odd number. Odd numbers
always have one left over. In a race, the first to finish is 1st, then 2nd, then 3rd. In Egypt
we pay with pounds and piastres. Some are coins and some are paper notes."
Watch Out For
The slip almost every child makes
Thinking big numbers are even and small ones odd. Size has nothing to do with it: 2 is
even, 19 is odd. The pairing test always decides.
Counting coins instead of money. Three coins can be worth more than five coins. A 1-
pound coin is worth four 25-piastre coins. Always look at what is written on the coin.
Try It at Home
Game 1 — The shoe rack (5 minutes)
Count the family's shoes by the door in twos: 2, 4, 6, 8... Is anyone's shoe missing? Then
take 7 spoons and try to pair them. Can you find an odd number that pairs up perfectly?
(He can't — let him keep trying and discover why.)
Game 2 — Toy car race and shop (10 minutes)
Race three toy cars down a sloping book: who came 1st, 2nd, 3rd? Then set up a shop
with real coins from your purse. Price a biscuit at 50 piastres. Which coins could he pay
with? Let him sort all the coins by what is written on them.

More examples to talk about
• Zero is even — nothing is left over! 20 is even too.
• The even numbers go 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 — every other number on the track.
• 15 can be broken up in many ways: 10 + 5, 9 + 6, 8 + 7, 12 + 3.
• Tricky: a 10-pound note is one piece of paper but is worth two 5-pound notes.
• Tricky: in the word SEIF, the 2nd letter is E and the 4th is F.
